stem: A client develops progressive weakness that began in the legs and is moving upward after a recent respiratory illness. Which condition is most concerning?

options.A: Myasthenia gravis, because it classically causes rapidly ascending symmetric weakness beginning in the legs after respiratory infection.
options.B: Multiple sclerosis, because it typically produces rapidly ascending symmetric paralysis with respiratory failure over days.
options.C: A localized musculoskeletal strain, because it best explains progressive bilateral weakness moving upward from the legs.
options.D: Guillain-Barré syndrome, with close monitoring for progression and respiratory muscle weakness.

rationale: Current NINDS guidance describes Guillain-Barré syndrome as an acute peripheral neuropathy in which weakness often begins in the feet or legs and progresses upward over hours to days, potentially involving the arms, face, and respiratory muscles. GBS also commonly begins days or weeks after a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. Because respiratory failure and autonomic instability can occur, hospitalized patients require close monitoring of progression, breathing, and cardiovascular status. Therefore D is correct. A, B, and C do not match the characteristic post-infectious rapidly progressive ascending weakness pattern.
educational_objective: Recognize rapidly progressive ascending weakness after a recent infection as a concerning pattern for Guillain-Barré syndrome and monitor closely for respiratory muscle involvement and other complications.
source_organization: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), NIH
source_version_date: Current NINDS disorder information and November 2024 fact sheet live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Symptoms: weakness often starts in feet/legs and may move upward to arms, face, and breathing muscles; progression occurs over hours/days. Risk/trigger section: often begins days or weeks after respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. Treatment/complications: monitor progression of weakness, breathing, heart rate; respiratory failure can occur.
source_claim_supported: Rapidly progressive ascending weakness beginning in the legs after a recent respiratory illness is characteristic of Guillain-Barré syndrome and warrants close monitoring for respiratory muscle weakness and other complications.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: recognize acute neurologic alterations, monitor respiratory status in neuromuscular weakness, identify life-threatening complications, and intervene for rapidly progressive physiologic deterioration.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — Guillain-Barré syndrome and respiratory-compromise risk

source_original.stem: A client develops progressive weakness that began in the legs and is moving upward after a recent respiratory illness. Which condition is most concerning?

options.A: Myasthenia gravis, which classically causes ascending symmetric weakness beginning in the legs after respiratory infection.
options.B: Multiple sclerosis, which typically produces rapidly ascending symmetric paralysis with respiratory failure over days.
options.C: A localized musculoskeletal strain, which best explains progressive bilateral weakness moving upward from the legs.
options.D: Guillain-Barré syndrome, with close monitoring for progression and respiratory muscle weakness.

source_original.rationale: Guillain-Barré syndrome often begins with weakness in the feet or legs that progresses upward and frequently follows a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. Respiratory failure can occur, so breathing and progression of weakness require close monitoring.
source_original.source_detail: Ascending weakness, post-infectious presentation, and respiratory monitoring Source has no separate formal version identifier in the cited page metadata; live currentness and applicability rechecked 2026-08-15. correction_summary: Retained the ascending-weakness construct and key D, tightened the distractors so they remain plausible neurologic/musculoskeletal alternatives without falsely sharing the classic GBS pattern, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a characteristic post-infectious syndrome plus an important respiratory-complication cue.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Guillain-Barré syndrome recognition and respiratory risk
audit_findings.source_authority: Current NINDS/NIH disorder guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: NINDS GBS disorder page and 2024 fact sheet live-rechecked 2026-08-16

audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses the source-supported post-infectious ascending weakness pattern and respiratory-risk monitoring without claiming that this vignette alone definitively diagnoses GBS.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because myasthenia gravis does not classically present as a post-infectious rapidly ascending leg-to-respiratory weakness syndrome.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because multiple sclerosis does not typically produce this acute symmetric ascending peripheral weakness pattern.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because a localized strain cannot explain progressive bilateral ascending neurologic weakness.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D matches the acute post-infectious ascending weakness pattern plus risk of respiratory-muscle involvement.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are clinical diagnoses/interpretations of the same weakness pattern; the correct answer depends on characteristic progression and trigger rather than a single isolated word.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — acute neuromuscular deterioration and respiratory-complication monitoring.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current NINDS GBS symptoms, post-infectious timing, respiratory and autonomic complications, all alternatives, rationale, objective, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. D remained uniquely correct.
